summary.text: For \(N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1\), modular exponentiations in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)[\sqrt3]\) show that \(2+\sqrt3\) has exact order \(N+1\) for every prime \(p\mid N\), using \(N+1=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}\) and separate nonidentity checks for its prime divisors \(2,3,100943\); since this unit group has fewer than \(p^2\) elements, every prime divisor satisfies \(p^2>N\), forcing \(N\) to be prime. Thus \(m=39101\) is a positive prime-producing step, so the relevant infimum cannot be zero.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 n=100943,\qquad L=2\cdot100943\cdot 3^{39101},\qquad N=L-1.
\]
We will prove that
\[
N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1
\]
is prime. Since this is precisely the number \(2n3^m-1\) with \(m=39101>0\), it follows that the set of admissible steps in the definition of \(a(100943)\) is nonempty, and hence that \(a(100943)\ne0\). Thus this one prime is a counterexample to the conjecture.

The main issue is proving the primality of the 18,662-digit integer \(N\). We do this with an \(N+1\) Lucas-type certificate in the quadratic algebra obtained by adjoining \(\sqrt3\).

## 1. Arithmetic in the quadratic algebra

For a modulus \(q\), write
\[
X_q=(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)[s]/(s^2-3).
\]
Thus an element is represented by a pair \((a,b)\), standing for \(a+bs\), and multiplication is
\[
(a,b)(c,d)=(ac+3bd,\ ad+bc)\pmod q.
\]
The identity is \((1,0)\). We use the element
\[
\alpha=(2,1)=2+s.
\]

All the large modular calculations below are performed first modulo \(N\). If a prime \(p\) divides \(N\), reduction modulo \(p\) carries every identity in \(X_N\) to the corresponding identity in \(X_p\).

For clarity, here is a completely explicit description of the finite powering computation used in the certificate. Define multiplication of pairs of least nonnegative residues modulo \(N\) by
\[
(a,b)\star(c,d)=
\bigl((ac+3bd)\bmod N,\ (ad+bc)\bmod N\bigr).
\]
For an exponent \(e\ge0\), compute \(\operatorname{Pow}(e)\) by the ordinary binary repeated-squaring algorithm:

* initialize \(B=(2,1)\), \(C=(1,0)\), and \(t=e\);
* while \(t>0\), if \(t\) is odd replace \(C\) by \(B\star C\); then replace \(B\) by \(B\star B\), and replace \(t\) by \(\lfloor t/2\rfloor\);
* when \(t=0\), output \(C\).

An induction on the number of processed binary digits shows that the output is exactly the least-residue pair representing \(\alpha^e\) in \(X_N\). More explicitly, after \(F\) binary digits have been processed, the current squared base represents
\[
\alpha^{2^F},
\]
and the accumulator represents
\[
\alpha^{e\bmod 2^F}.
\]
This proves the correctness of the calculation without making any assumption about the primality of \(N\).

For memory convenience the actual calculation was divided into blocks of 1000 binary digits. Chaining blocks is legitimate because if a block begins with a pair representing \(\alpha^t\), then after \(F\) squarings its new base represents \(\alpha^{t2^F}\), while multiplying into the accumulator according to the low \(F\) bits of an integer \(e\) adds the exponent \(t(e\bmod2^F)\). Sixty-two such blocks, followed by the short final blocks needed for the three quotient exponents, give the following certificate.

Define the six integers \(A_2,A_3,B_3,A_k,B_k\), all in the interval \([0,N-1]\), by the exact repeated-squaring outputs
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pow}(L/2)&=(A_2,0),\\
\operatorname{Pow}(L/3)&=(A_3,B_3),\\
\operatorname{Pow}(L/100943)&=(A_k,B_k).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are not existentially chosen numbers: the recurrence above is an explicit deterministic construction of their decimal expansions. For reference, their sizes and identifying initial and final decimal digits are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 &\text{number of digits}&\text{initial digits}&\text{final digits}\\ \hline
A_2&18662&167219529406&323395721656\\
A_3&18661&836097647030&661697860828\\
B_3&18662&130330650125&919490145778\\
A_k&18662&141553338102&074391079186\\
B_k&18662&123992859189&732486786003.
\end{array}
\]
The repeated-squaring calculation, followed in the gcd assertions by the ordinary Euclidean algorithm, gives
\[
 A_2^2\equiv1\pmod N                                                   \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\gcd\bigl(\gcd(A_2+N-1,0),N\bigr)&=1,\\
\gcd\bigl(\gcd(A_3+N-1,B_3),N\bigr)&=1,\\
\gcd\bigl(\gcd(A_k+N-1,B_k),N\bigr)&=1.                 \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
These are finite integer computations. Their mathematical role is important: (1) supplies \(\alpha^L=1\), while the three Euclidean-algorithm identities in (2) prove that none of the three quotient powers can become \(1\) modulo any prime factor of \(N\).

Indeed, the definitions of the residues and (1) give in \(X_N\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha^{L/2}&=(A_2,0),\\
\alpha^{L/3}&=(A_3,B_3),\\
\alpha^{L/100943}&=(A_k,B_k),                              \tag{3}\\
\alpha^L&=(A_2,0)^2=(1,0).                                 \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
The last equality uses \(L=2(L/2)\), the multiplication rule for pairs, and (1).

## 2. The abstract \(N+1\) primality argument

We now prove the criterion that turns (2)--(4) into primality.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(N\) is composite, and let \(p\) be its least prime factor. Then
\[
p^2\le N.                                                   \tag{5}
\]
To see this, write \(N=pc\). Since \(N\) is composite, \(c>1\); every integer greater than one has a prime divisor, and by minimality of \(p\), every prime divisor of \(c\) is at least \(p\). Hence \(c\ge p\), proving (5).

Reduce (4) modulo \(p\). It says
\[
\alpha^L=1\quad\text{in }X_p.                              \tag{6}
\]
Consequently \(\alpha\) is a unit in \(X_p\): an explicit inverse is \(\alpha^{L-1}\). Let \(d\) be its multiplicative order. Equation (6) implies \(d\mid L\).

We claim that for every prime \(r\mid L\),
\[
\alpha^{L/r}\ne1\quad\text{in }X_p.                        \tag{7}
\]
For any one of the quotient powers in (3), let its two integer coordinates be \((x,y)\). If its reduction modulo \(p\) were \((1,0)\), then
\[
p\mid x-1\quad\text{and}\quad p\mid y.
\]
Because \(p\mid N\), the first divisibility is equivalently
\[
p\mid x+(N-1).
\]
Thus \(p\) would divide each of \(x+(N-1),y,N\), and would therefore divide
\[
\gcd\bigl(\gcd(x+N-1,y),N\bigr).
\]
For each of the three coordinate pairs this gcd is 1 by (2), an impossibility. This proves (7), once it is known that the three listed primes exhaust the prime divisors of \(L\).

That exhaustion is straightforward. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{100943}<318\) shows that \(100943\) is prime. Therefore, from
\[
L=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101},
\]
every prime divisor of \(L\) is one of
\[
2,\quad3,\quad100943.
\]
More explicitly, if a prime \(r\) divides this product, Euclid's lemma first places it in \(2\cdot100943\) or in \(3^{39101}\). In the former case another application puts it in \(2\) or \(100943\), so primality forces equality with one of those factors. In the latter case a prime dividing a power of 3 divides 3, and hence equals 3. Thus the three cases represented in (3) are exhaustive.

It follows that the order \(d\) of \(\alpha\) is exactly \(L\). Here is the standard order argument in detail. We already know \(d\mid L\). If \(d<L\), then \(L/d>1\), so choose a prime \(r\mid L/d\). Then \(d\mid L/r\), which would imply
\(
\alpha^{L/r}=1,
\)
contrary to (7). Hence
\[
d=L=N+1.                                                    \tag{8}
\]

On the other hand, the underlying set of \(X_p\) has exactly \(p^2\) elements, since each of its two coordinates has \(p\) choices. Its unit group has strictly fewer than \(p^2\) elements, because at least the zero pair is not a unit. The order of an element of a finite group cannot exceed the number of elements in that group. Applying this to \(\alpha\) and using (8),
\[
N+1=L=d\le |X_p^\times|<p^2.                               \tag{9}
\]
But (5) says \(p^2\le N\), contradicting (9). Therefore \(N\) cannot be composite. Since plainly \(N\ge2\), it follows that
\[
\boxed{2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1\text{ is prime}.}
\]

## 3. Consequence for the sequence

For \(n=100943\), let
\[
S=\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2\cdot100943\cdot3^m-1
\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
The primality just proved shows that
\[
39101\in S.
\]
Thus \(S\) is nonempty. Every member of \(S\) is positive. By the well-ordering principle a nonempty subset of the natural numbers has a least member, and that least member is itself in the set; hence it is positive. By the definition of A354747,
\[
a(100943)=\min S>0.
\]
In particular,
\[
\boxed{a(100943)\ne0}.
\]
This disproves the conjecture \(a(100943)=0\). Notice that the argument does not assert that \(39101\) is the least successful exponent; no such assertion is needed. Its role is to exhibit one successful exponent, which already rules out the value zero.
